Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
FISHERIES IMPACT ASSESSMENT
Introduction
This section presents a review of the baseline fisheries conditions within the
Assessment Area, and the results of the potential fisheries impact assessment relating
to the construction and operation of the Project. The location plan and description of
the Project are presented in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 2.1 and Chapter 2, respectively.
In accordance with the EIAO-TM, baseline conditions for fisheries resources were
evaluated using information from available literature and site visits conducted for the
purposes of this EIA. Measures required to mitigate any identified adverse impacts are
recommended, where appropriate, and residual impacts are assessed.
Environmental Legislation, Standards and Guidelines
This fisheries impact assessment makes reference to the following HKSAR
Government ordinances, regulations, standards, guidelines, and documents when
identifying the importance of fisheries resources, and evaluating and assessing
potential impacts arising from the Project:-
• EIA Study Brief (ESB-375/2025) issued for the proposed project, Development of
the Loop – Eastern Connection Road
• Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (EIAO) (Cap. 499) and subsidiary
legislation and guidelines
• Technical Memorandum on Environmental Impact Assessment Process (EIAO-
TM) Annexes 9 and 17
• EIAO Guidance Note No. 15/2023 – Methodologies for Fisheries Baseline
Surveys
• Water Pollution Control Ordinance (Cap. 358)
Assessment Methodology
Assessment Area
In accordance with the EIA Study Brief No. ESB-375/2025, the Assessment Area for
fisheries impacts includes areas within 500 metres from the boundary of the Project
and associated works, and other areas that would be potentially impacted by the
construction or operation of the Project. Special attention is also given to pond culture
resources and activities, as well as any watercourses which may serve as water
sources for the fishpond areas. The Assessment Area is shown in
60722948/A10/FIGURE 9.1.
Literature review and desktop study were conducted to collate the latest baseline
conditions regarding fisheries resources within the Assessment Area. The review
included:-
• Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) Annual Reports;
• AFCD website on aquaculture;

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)

• AFCD website on Accredited Fish Farm Scheme;
• Report of the Committee on Sustainable Fisheries (2010);
• EIA Report for Development of Lok Ma Chau Loop – EIA Report (AEIAR-
176/2013) (CEDD & PlanD, 2013a); and
• EIA Report for North East New Territories New Development Areas Planning and
Engineering Study – Investigation – EIA Report (AEIAR-175/2013) (CEDD &
PlanD, 2013b).
In addition to reviewing recent aerial photographs, site visits were conducted between
July 2022 to December 2023 to verify the condition of ponds and their associated
fisheries activities, with particular focus on those within the Project Boundary, where
accessible. The conditions of the fishponds and the fisheries activities were observed
and recorded. The actual pond status was then further updated based on information
obtained from AFCD.
Assessment for Pond Culture Fisheries
The status of fishpond management was investigated with reference to the evidence of
aquaculture activities, such as the presence of fisheries operations (e.g. stocking,
feeding, harvesting), management activities (e.g. pumping of water, draining, dredging,
re-profiling, and maintenance grass trimming), and the presence and conditions of
associated equipment (e.g. aerators, conditions of pond bund, fodder). Attention was
also given to any watercourses which potentially serve as water sources for fishponds.
Ponds in the Assessment Area were assigned to one of the following categories:
• Active: currently utilised for commercial aquaculture activities (described in
Section 9.3.6), including commercial fishponds, fish fry ponds, and indoor fish
farms;
• Inactive: no current commercial aquaculture activities and management (e.g.
overgrown vegetation at pond bunds which hindered culture activities, and lack
of equipment such as aerator), but no major physical constraints to its resumption
in the short-term, including fishponds with fish present in non-commercial
quantities and ponds for recreational fishing or water sports;
• Abandoned: ponds in which there was physical evidence that aquaculture has not
been practised for many years (typically ponds with overgrown vegetation or dried
up) and/or where there are obvious physical constraints to the resumption of
fisheries activities (e.g. inaccessible or fenced off).
Assessment Approach
The criteria and guidelines set out in Annexes 9 and 17 of the EIAO-TM were followed
to evaluate and assess the impact of Project construction and operation on the fisheries
resources. Potential direct / indirect, on-site / off-site, primary, secondary, cumulative
and residual fisheries impacts arising from the construction and operation of the Project
were identified and evaluated. Mitigation measures as well as environmental
monitoring and auditing programme were recommended, where necessary.

Baseline Conditions
Pond Culture Fisheries Activities and Resources
Desktop Study
The pond fish / aquaculture industry of Hong Kong is mainly centred in the northwest
New Territories. The northern portion of the Project site and the Assessment Area falls
partially within this area of aquaculture activities.
According to AFCD (2024a), local inland fishponds covered approximately 1,119 ha in
2024. These ponds produced 1,349 tonnes of freshwater fish with a value of HK$37
million. The latest available data shows that production from local fishponds accounted
for about 2% of the total local freshwater fish consumption in 2023 (AFCD, 2023a).
The vast majority of local fishponds engaged in carp polyculture and farmed species
such as Bighead Carp, Grass Carp, Common Carp and Silver Carp in combination with
Tilapia or Grey Mullet. A small portion (about 11%) of pond fish culture in Hong Kong
involve monoculture of carnivorous species such as giant groupers, seabreams, and
spotted scats at brackish fishponds near the coastline (AFCD, 2024). The aquaculture
species Jade Perch (Scortum barcoo) was introduced by AFCD to the local fisheries
industry (AFCD, 2011). Since 2010, AFCD has mastered the induced spawning and fry
rearing techniques and was able to produce Jade Perch fry in mass quantity, reducing
fry cost and maintaining the supply of fry (AFCD, 2023b). A voluntary Accredited Fish
Farm Scheme (AFFS) has been introduced by AFCD to enhance the environmental
hygiene standards of local aquaculture farms and the quality of aquaculture products
(AFCD, 2024b).
Fishponds farms have been gradually declining in number since the 1970s, especially
in the Deep Bay area as these farms are being abandoned and/or replaced by urban
development. Table 9.1 presents the AFCD figures on fishpond area and annual fish
production in Hong Kong from 2014 to 2024.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Under the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Study for the Development of the
Loop (the Loop) (CEDD & PlanD, 2013a), site visits were conducted between 2009 and
2010 to investigate the fisheries status of ponds. No fishponds were identified within
the Loop, as they were filled and lost after the Shenzhen River Regulation Project, and
the area within the Loop was not actively managed and was considered as marshes,
dominated by emergent vegetation (prior to the development of the Loop). A mixture of
active, inactive and abandoned ponds was identified to the south of the Loop. (CEDD
& PlanD, 2013a).
The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) commenced a
Strategic Feasibility Study on the Development of Wetland Conservation Parks System
in August 2022 which was completed in October 2024. The Strategic Feasibility Study
has reviewed the ecological conditions, land use and planning aspects, aquaculture
activities, as well as eco-education and recreational facilities within the proposed
Wetland Conservation Parks (WCPs) areas. The proposed Hoo Hok Wai (HHW) WCP,
which also covers the San Lau / Nam Hang (SL/NH) area, has the general theme of “A
Rural Retreat”. Within the proposed HHW WCP, the existing network of fishponds will
largely be retained but zoned and managed to enhance the area’s ecological capacity
while promoting the sustainable modernisation of aquaculture practices. Rural activities
such as leisure farming may also be introduced to allow visitors to experience a rural
lifestyle and enjoy the idyllic countryside landscape.
Recent Site Visit Findings
Hoo Hok Wai is a core fishpond area in Hong Kong, with many ponds remaining under
active production. Aquaculture activities such as drying of ponds, reprofiling, harvesting
and feeding were frequently observed. Some ponds, however, were inactive or
abandoned; these ponds usually covered with dense vegetation and show no sign of
commercial aquaculture activity. Currently, a total of 96 ponds were identified fully or
partially within the 500m Assessment Area of the Project, including 71 active fishponds,
7 inactive fishponds and 18 abandoned fishponds. The majority of active fishponds
were aggregated at the northern and northwestern of the Project Boundary, while some
active ponds were also recorded alongside the current boundary fence road, to the
south of the Loop. Inactive and abandoned fishponds were recorded scattered across
the Assessment Area, with some larger inactive and abandoned fishponds located
south of the Loop.
Fishponds throughout the HHW fall on both government and private land, with only a
few scattered government or private land areas. This is because the lot index plan does
not specifically define boundaries based on ponds. For those fishponds found to be
gated or remained inaccessible, satellite and drone images were reviewed to determine
their status (Table 9.2 refers).
A total of two inactive fishponds and one active fishpond were recorded within the
Project Boundary, namely Pond 36 – 38 (60722948/A10/FIGURE 9.1 refers). Pond 36
(about 1.55 ha) which is currently located mostly on government-owned land, and
partially on private lots, has recently been reprofiled and resumed aquaculture activity.
Equipment such as aerators related to fisheries operation were observed within the
fishpond. Whereas the two Ponds 37-38 (of about 3.07 ha in total) adjacent to Pond 36
were observed to be inactive and gradually becoming overgrown with wetland
vegetation. The physical condition of these ponds is generally poor due to lack of
management. Approximately 0.14 ha pond bunds of three abandoned ponds (Ponds
39, 39a, and 93) were also recorded partially falling within the Project Boundary.

pond habitat impacted under Phase 1, whereas only about 0.03 ha of pond bund from
Pond 93 will be impacted under Phase 2. Overall, approximately 1.51 ha of pond habitat
will be impacted during construction phase, and the associated construction works at
Pond 36-38 would include draining the water in ponds before commencement of any
excavation and construction works.
Enhancement measures, such as frequent pond drain downs and temporary fish
stocking, would be implemented in the remaining area of Pond 36-38, to retain its
functional value and maintain its attractiveness to waterbirds and other wetland-
dependent species during the construction phase. This includes approximately 1.21
ha of active fishpond and 2.08 ha of inactive fishpond, totally to approximately 3.29 ha.
A temporary aboveground wildlife crossing will be provided above the construction area
through Pond 36-37, as illustrated in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 9.2. The crossing
(approximately 40 m wide) will include a central water feature and dense shrub planting
along the edges to minimise disturbance and facilitate wildlife movement (e.g. Eurasian
Otter). The structure will temporarily occupy part of existing fishponds, and the
corresponding temporary loss have already been assessed for direct impact due to
construction works, therefore no additional impact on pond and fish production are
anticipated. Upon completion of the underpass roads, the excavation cofferdam will be
backfilled and fully enclosed, and the Ecological Area (EA), the Meander, and fishponds
will be reinstated by the Contractor. In addition, Pond 36 -38 will be converted as
ecological enhanced ponds. Therefore, permanent loss of fishponds or reduction in
aquaculture production is expected.
As mentioned in Section 8 of this Report, under the phased approach to construction
of the Project, the ecological impacts resulting from the loss of pond habitat shall be
compensated using existing Offsite Wetland Compensation Areas of the Loop (i.e.
OWCA Areas 2 and 9). However, about 0.24 ha of active pond from Pond 36 would
still be subject to potential loss of fisheries production due to construction works.
Although Pond 36 has been reprofiled since site checks conducted in October 2024,
and equipment such as aerators were observed within the fishpond during site check
at October 2025 (Section 9.4.9 refers), the pond was previously identified as inactive.
No obvious fisheries activity observed and most areas of the pond were dry during site
visits conducted between July 2022 to December 2023. Consolidating previous and
recent observation, it is anticipated that the current commercial fish production had only
just commenced at the time of this assessment and the potential contribution to the
annual fisheries production in Hong Kong would be low, hence the impact to fisheries
production is considered of negligible during the construction phase. Meanwhile, no
evidence of commercial aquaculture activities was observed in Ponds 37–38. Therefore,
the temporary impact on aquaculture activities is considered negligible.
Identification of Potential Impacts from Construction-Indirect Impacts
Deterioration of Water Quality and Hydrological Condition
Indirect water quality impact from construction activities may affect the survival of
cultured fish. For example, accidental spills of oils and other chemicals could affect
aquatic organisms (including aquaculture fisheries), resulting in lethal / sublethal
impacts (e.g. direct mortality, reproductive retardation). Removal of vegetation during
site formation could also elevate sediment levels in site runoff, increasing suspended
solids (SS) level in the aquatic environment. Furthermore, discharge from land-based
construction works (e.g. excavated materials and sediments from construction works
in ponds, general cleaning and polishing, wheel washing, dust suppression, utility
installation, etc.) and construction site runoff (e.g. runoff and erosion of exposed bare

Mitigation measures will be implemented to control runoff and drainage from the
construction site, as well as the adoption of guidelines and good site practices for
handling and disposal of construction discharges, excavated materials and sediments
(refer to Chapters 5 and 6). Unacceptable impacts on water quality, and the associated
potential indirect injury / mortality on cultured fish are not expected.
Bund Stability and Water Seepage
Construction activities that occur adjacent or in close vicinity to fishponds may result in
indirect impacts on these fishponds by affecting the stability of the pond bund,
potentially resulting in instability of the pond structure, or water seepage. In the absence
of mitigation measures, this could inhibit pond usage and result in potentially minor to
moderate impacts on the remaining ponds adjacent to the development boundary. With
appropriate mitigation measures (i.e. sheet pile wall) implemented to ensure the
stability of the pond bund during construction phase, adverse impacts on aquaculture
activities are not anticipated.
Blockage of Existing Access
Proposed construction works may potentially restrict pond operators’ access to
fishponds, which could affect the implementation of management strategies and the
yield of fisheries. Without mitigation measures, this may result in minor to moderate
impact on fishpond area. Mitigation measures (e.g. provision of temporary road and
access arrangement) would be in place to minimise the potential blockage and the
associated impact on fishpond area.
Dumping of Construction Waste
Dumping of construction waste or excavated material on fishponds other than those
already indicated as requiring draining for construction purposes could cause a direct
impact on pond fisheries. No direct dumping of waste from these construction works
will be allowed, no unacceptable impact would be expected.
Operational Phase
Upon completion of the Project, Pond 36-38 (hereafter referred to as Area 4) will be
converted as ecological enhanced ponds of approximately 4.63 ha, which will enhance
the ecological value and function of these ponds, supporting species of conservation
interest. However, a small portion of Pond 38 (approximately 0.25 ha) will be
permanently lost under the Project Alignment due to the construction of the ventilation
opening and maintenance access. Therefore, the final area of Area 4 to be ecological
enhanced ponds will be of 4.38 ha.
Although ponds under Area 4 will be reinstated as ecological enhanced ponds, area
loss of about 4.38 ha for fisheries production is anticipated (as the primary function of
these ponds would be for ecological habitat provision). Given that Pond 37-38 are
inactive ponds with no fisheries production expected (Section 9.5.4 refers), and that
Pond 36 only resumed fisheries production recently, it is expected that the contribution
of fisheries production from Area 4 is relatively low, therefore the overall impact on the
loss of fisheries production under the Project is considered negligible. No further

Surface Runoff
Surface runoff from the ECR could potentially cause impacts on nearby water bodies.
The presence of oil, grease and grit on surfaces of road, as well as cleaning agents
used for road washing may affect the water quality of nearby waterbodies (e.g., entering
nearby drainage system or watercourse). With reference to Section 5, with proper
implementation of recommended measures, no adverse water quality impact from
surface runoff on fishpond water quality and fisheries production are anticipated.
Bund Stability and Water Seepage
The temporarily affected fishponds will be reinstated upon completion of the ECR,
therefore, no adverse impacts on the stability of pond structures or water seepage
issues seepage are anticipated.
Blockage of Existing Access
There is concern on blockage of existing paths to active fishponds during the
operational phase (i.e. blocked by proposed connection roads). The ECR design has
included connections to existing access points to the HHW area, therefore no long-term
impacts to pond operators accessing fishpond areas are expected.
Impacts to Capture Fisheries
No capture fisheries are present within the Study Area and as such no impacts are
predicted to capture fisheries in the construction or operational stages of this Project.
Impacts to Water Systems of Fisheries Importance
Given the distance to the closest water systems of fisheries importance (e.g. Deep Bay)
from the Assessment Area, is approximately 10km, it is considered that construction
and/or operational impacts to water systems of fisheries importance are insignificant.
Summary of Fisheries Impact
Overall, the temporary and permanent loss of fisheries resources / production from the
Project would comprise 1.51 ha and 4.63 ha of ponds respectively. At a cumulative
maximum of slightly more than 0.4% of the overall fishpond area in the northwest NT,
this is considered a negligible impact to fisheries production. Details of both
construction and operation phase fisheries impact under the Project are shown in
60722948/A10/FIGURE 9.2 and summarised in Table 9.3 and Table 9.4 below.

Cumulative Impact
The committed major development projects, such as San Tin / Lok Ma Chau
Development Node (hereafter referred as the ST/LMC DN) within the project vicinity,
would not result in indirect loss of fishponds within the Assessment Area. Fishpond loss
arising from the ST/LMC DN would be compensated by establishing the Sam Po Shue
WCP which has reserved 40 ha of fisheries enhancement area solely for aquaculture
use. Since this project is not predicted to cause significant fisheries impact (i.e. no large
area of active fishpond would be affected permanently), there is no potential for
significant cumulative impacts within the project vicinity.

2.

Chapter 6), and thus such impact is not predicted to occur.

fishponds after commencement of site works. The sheet pile wall should be constructed
by silent piling method (Press-in method) which induces minimal vibration. Therefore,
the stability of the fishpond bund will not be influenced by the construction of the sheet
pile wall. In the event of excessive groundwater infiltration being observed during
underpass / depressed road construction, grouting should be applied as far as
practicable to limit the groundwater inflow to acceptable levels. With these measures,
significant impacts are not anticipated. No operational impacts anticipated.
Blockage of Access Roads to Fishponds
Temporary traffic arrangements will be implemented to ensure the continued or
alternative provision of access to fishponds throughout the construction phase. Detailed
arrangement cannot be provided at this stage, but the project proponent will be
responsible for drawing up such an arrangement with the contractor as and when
necessary, throughout the construction period. Subsequently, access to the fishponds
would be provided in the operational phase.
Good Site Practices
Standard mitigation measures to control site runoff and other pollutants (e.g. dust)
caused by construction activities and good site practices will be implemented during
the construction phase of the Project. Excavated material and other inert construction
wastes produced will be transferred to proper recipients (i.e. landfill) (see Section 6).
Sewage from the construction work force will be dealt with via a sewerage system and
will not be discharged directly to surrounding water bodies. With these measures,
indirect impacts on fisheries due to construction activities will be insignificant (for details
of measures protecting nearby water bodies including fishponds (see Section 5).
Compensation
Loss of Pond Areas
Permanent loss of a small area of 0.25 ha inactive fishpond due to the footprint of the
ventilation opening and associated maintenance access required for the underpass
section of the Project Alignment is considered to be a negligible impact, in view of the
small contribution to the total fishpond area in Hong Kong (below 0.1%). It is considered
that no mitigation is required for this loss.
Secondary Impact from Wetland Compensation
As described in Sections 9.5.10 – 9.5.11, following completion of the ECR, Area 4 will
be subject to ecological enhancement measures and converted into ecological
enhanced ponds. Considering that the existing Pond 37 – 38 are inactive ponds, and
that Pond 36 only resumed fisheries production recently, the impact on fisheries
production is therefore considered negligible. No further mitigation for these impacts
to fisheries production are therefore required.
Evaluation of Residual Impacts and Environmental Monitoring and Audit
With the above measures in place, along with measures for mitigating water quality
impacts and managing waste, no residual fisheries impacts are expected.
With the implementation of monitoring and audit for water quality, no specific
programme for fisheries is deemed necessary.

Conclusion
Since the pond areas to be lost do not account for a significant proportion of the total
fishpond area in Hong Kong, the fisheries impact is considered to be negligible. Indirect
impacts arising from construction activities and operation of the proposed development
would be properly mitigated through standard practices and thus no significant fisheries
impact is anticipated. Overall, no unacceptable fisheries impact is predicted from this
project.
